summary: A Network Host Status report from Ellen Westheimer of BBN covering April 10 to April 21, 1972. The USC IBM 360/44 was connected to the network, and a terminal IMP was installed at Global Weather Central in Omaha on April 18. It updates RFC 330. It was replaced by RFC 342.

eli5.summary: This is like a school attendance sheet for the early internet. Someone wrote down which big computers were switched on and ready to help, and which ones were not, so people knew where to go.

subtitle: ARPANET host availability report for April 1972

tldr.problem: ARPANET operators needed to know which hosts were up and available, and track their status over time.
tldr.mechanism: A test procedure probed each host regularly and recorded its status. Ellen Westheimer at BBN published weekly status reports with dates, times, and coded results (Open, Dead, Refused, Half Open, Full) for each site.
tldr.outcome: Operators could see which hosts were available for users to connect to, and troubleshoot problems.

facts.label: Status codes
facts.value: O, D, T, H, F, R

today: RFC 332 is historic and was replaced by RFC 342. These host status reports were the precursor to modern monitoring and status pages that track the availability of network services.

sections.title: Host Status Reporting
sections.content:
RFC 332 reports the network host status for April 10-21, 1972, covering most ARPANET hosts during this period. This was part of regular monitoring by the Network Control Center at BBN to track which hosts were available and functioning.

The report covers a time when the USC IBM 360/44 was newly connected to the network (April 10) and a Terminal IMP was installed at Global Weather Central in Omaha (April 18).
sections.eli5: Each day, someone called each computer and noted whether it answered. This report shows the results for two weeks.

sections.title: Host Categories
sections.content:
Hosts fell into different categories: regular servers (always expected to be available), hosts not yet expected to function as servers, and user-only hosts (including Terminal IMPs at AMES, MITRE, NBS, ETAC, USC, and GWC). User-only hosts could not serve requests from other sites; they could only send requests themselves.

The Network Control Center computer itself was marked user-only because it was used solely for gathering network statistics.
sections.eli5: Some computers were like restaurants, waiting to serve other people. Others were like customers, just asking for service. The report said which was which.

sections.title: Status Codes
sections.content:
The report used status codes to describe each host's behavior during a daily test:

  • O (Open): Host opened a connection and was accessible to users.
  • D (Dead): Host was dead or inaccessible from the test point.
  • T (Half Open): Host opened a connection but then closed it immediately or did not respond further.
  • H (Half Open variant): Alternative notation for half-open states.
  • F (Full): Host opened a connection but reported all ports were in use.
  • R (Refused): Host sent a CLS (close) in response to the test.
sections.eli5: O meant the computer answered and worked. D meant it did not pick up. T and H meant it started to answer but then hung up. F meant all its lines were busy. R meant it said no thanks.

sections.title: Publication and Use
sections.content: These status reports were published regularly by Ellen Westheimer at BBN. Network users would consult them to find available hosts and to understand why they could not reach a particular site. The reports also helped network operators spot recurring problems and plan maintenance.
sections.eli5: The reports let users plan their work: if one computer was broken, they could use a different one.
